newsitem.title: FRANCE: French magistrates welcome Chirac reform plan.
newsitem.headline: French magistrates welcome Chirac reform plan.

text.p: French magistrates on Friday welcomed President Jacques Chirac's plans to bolster the independence of the judiciary but some questioned his determination to get to the heart of sleaze in French politics.
In a televised interview on Thursday, Chirac said he wanted the centre-right cabinet to initiate radical reform aimed at making public prosecutors independent of the Justice Ministry.

The daily Le Monde said Chirac had broken "a very French judicial taboo" with the idea of scrapping a system that makes prosecutors subordinate to the Ministry -- and open to charges of political manipulation.

The government caused an outcry last month by chartering a helicopter in a vain attempt to track down a prosecutor trekking in the Himalayas to discuss a probe opened by his zealous deputy against the wife of the mayor of Paris.

Justice Minister Jacques Toubon said it had been necessary to check whether the probe did not contradict the prosecutor's instructions. Ths scandal caused charges that the government was trying to block an embarrassing probe.
Judges and magistrates generally welcomed the planned reform and said they would help the work of any commission set up.
Toubon said the commission of legal experts, perhaps led by the head of the Supreme Court, would be set up in coming days.

But some experts worried Chirac's announcement was window-dressing at a time when all political parties, including the Rally for the Republic (RPR) Chirac founded in 1976, are increasingly targeted by political funding scandals.

"We will ensure that the work is not buried," said Valery Turcey, head of the centrist Union Syndicale des Magistrats welcoming the proposed reform. He said the RPR was "ringed on all sides by the multiplication of corruption cases."
The leftist Syndicat de la Magistrature also said Chirac's proposal was "interesting".

The right-wing APM magistrates' group, close to Toubon, expressed concern that cutting the link between prosecutors and the ministry could create an Italian-style system that it said would let prosecutors act with too little control.
At the same time as considering reform of the judicial hierarchy, Chirac said he wanted to strengthen the presumption of innocence until any suspect was proven guilty.

Some magistrates feared this could muzzle investigators and the media, making it easier to hush up politically-embarrassing cases. Chirac also said he wanted to reduce bureaucratic hurdles that make it too expensive to prosecute minor crimes.
